feedback: If a learner expects input to equal Q, prompt them to identify where energy goes besides the water — air, beaker, evaporation — so the experiment is less than 100% efficient and input exceeds Q.
If a learner plugs in the final temperature, point to both the start and final readings and have them subtract before substituting: ΔT = final − start.
If the thermometer bulb is not fully immersed or is read at an angle, ask what error that introduces and have them correct the technique.
Ask: 'Your measured input is bigger than the Q you calculated — is that a mistake or expected, and why?' to surface loss reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: The electrical energy supplied is more than the Q reaching the substance because real experiments lose energy to the surroundings; naming and reducing those losses is the core evaluative skill, and ΔT is a difference, not a final reading.
learnerActions: Set a known mass of water (weighed on a balance) in a beaker with an immersion heater/joulemeter, thermometer and stopwatch.
Switch on and record the temperature at regular time intervals while noting the energy supplied (power × time, or the joulemeter reading).
Compute ΔT as the CHANGE (final minus start, not a single reading) and calculate Q = mcΔT.

Compare the electrical energy you put in with the Q you calculated; it is usually larger, so explain why, and if it is not, look for measurement problems such as thermometer lag or heat gained from the room.

Name specific losses (heat to the air, the beaker, evaporation) and propose and, if possible, test improvements (lid, insulation/lagging, starting below and ending above room temperature, accounting for the container).
Read the thermometer at eye level with the bulb fully immersed, and note where lag or uneven heating could introduce error.
activities.title: Hands-on heating practical: measure energy and evaluate error

feedback: If a learner treats c as 'how hot something gets', re-anchor it as energy per kilogram per degree — a fixed property of the material.

If a learner says the hottest sample must have received the most energy, remind them the energy was identical and the difference is c (aluminium has the lowest c, so it rises most; water the highest c, so it rises least).
activities.intendedInsight: Specific heat capacity is a property of the material (energy needed per kilogram per degree), independent of how much you have; with the same energy and the same mass, a lower-c material rises more, so temperature change is not the same as energy supplied.
learnerActions: Give equal masses of water, oil and aluminium the identical energy input, side by side.
Record and compare the different temperature rises reached by each material.
Work back to a measured c for each and relate it to how 'stubborn to heat' the material is.
State in your own words why a bigger temperature rise does not by itself mean more energy was supplied.
activities.title: Same energy, three materials

feedback: If the learner cannot say where energy went, list candidate sinks (air, beaker, evaporation) and ask which they could reduce.
If the learner uses a final reading as ΔT, have them mark start and end and subtract.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating where energy was lost, and distinguishing ΔT from a final reading, consolidates the evaluative reasoning behind the measurement.
learnerActions: Predict what c you expect before computing it, then compare with the measured value.
Answer a lab-partner's questions: 'Your value for c is bigger than the textbook's — where did the missing energy go?'
Explain what lagging would change, and whether ΔT is the change or the final reading.
Justify your reasoning about why the input exceeds Q.
activities.title: Socratic debrief on the result

feedback: For a ΔT error, confirm ΔT = final − start and have them recompute.
For a 'too high c' item, confirm the cause is energy lost to the surroundings so less reached the substance than was counted.
Keep numbers friendly so arithmetic does not obscure the physics.
activities.intendedInsight: The calculations, gradient-reading and error-identification are well-defined skills that also surface the temperature-vs-energy and ΔT-vs-final-temperature misconceptions.
learnerActions: Apply Q = mcΔT both directions: find Q for a given rise, find ΔT for a given energy, and back out c from measured values.
Read the heating rate from the gradient of a temperature–time graph.
Answer 'why did the measured c come out too high?' and justify (energy lost to surroundings).
Sort changes by whether they raise or lower the temperature rise for a fixed energy (e.g. more mass, higher-c material → smaller rise).
Spot the slip of using the final temperature instead of ΔT.
activities.title: Calculation and graph-reading practice
